overview: Grape downy mildew is caused by Plasmopara viticola, an oomycete rather than a true fungus. Yellowish, sometimes oily angular lesions and white growth on the leaf underside are described by Penn State Extension. Warm, wet conditions favor infection.
symptoms: Angular yellowish or oily-looking leaf lesions
White cottony growth may appear underneath leaves
favorable_conditions: Warm, wet conditions and prolonged leaf wetness
spread: Rain and wet periods support infection and repeated disease cycles
prevention: Improve canopy airflow and leaf drying where appropriate
Manage infected leaf debris using regional guidance
management: Use only locally registered products according to their label and extension advice
professional_help_message: This image classification is not a field diagnosis. Ask a local agricultural extension service or plant diagnostic laboratory to confirm the cause before choosing treatment.

overview: Powdery mildew can affect green grapevine tissues and appear as whitish-gray powder on leaves and shoots.
symptoms: Whitish-gray dusty growth on upper or lower leaf surfaces
Leaves and shoots may be affected
possible_causes: Powdery mildew fungi; species depend on host and region
prevention: Maintain an open canopy using locally appropriate pruning and shoot positioning
management: Confirm the disease and consult local grape guidance before treatment
Follow product labels and regional registration requirements
professional_help_message: This image classification is not a field diagnosis. Ask a local agricultural extension service or plant diagnostic laboratory to confirm the cause before choosing treatment.

overview: Esca is associated with a complex of wood-infecting fungi; leaf symptoms can include interveinal striping and vary between seasons.
symptoms: Interveinal striping that can dry or become necrotic
management: Have affected vines assessed by a viticulture or plant-health specialist
Do not infer vine-wide disease from one leaf image
professional_help_message: This image classification is not a field diagnosis. Ask a local agricultural extension service or plant diagnostic laboratory to confirm the cause before choosing treatment.

management: UC IPM notes control may not be warranted when feeding does not affect yield; ask local experts if damage is extensive
